gallery.title: File:Dashavtar Ivory Carving.jpg
gallery.description:
Carved in ivory, these figurines depict Vishnu's 10 'avatars' from Hindu Mythology. This artifact, which is displayed in the National Museum (New Delhi) is from around late 18th Century south India. Representing Hindu god Vishnu's ten major avatars (from top). Matsya; Kurma; Varaha; Narasimha; Vamana; Parashurama; Rama; Balarama (lowest line left center with club); Krishna (lowest line right center with whip) and Kalki
Image taken by Noman.

gallery.filename: Exhibit of Photographs of North-Eastern Tribes in National Museum of India.jpg
gallery.title: File:Exhibit of Photographs of North-Eastern Tribes in National Museum of India.jpg
gallery.source: Exhibit of Photographs of North-Eastern Tribes in National Museum of India
gallery.description: This image showcases an exhibit displayed at the National Museum of India. The exhibit features a carefully curated collection of black-and-white photographs depicting the everyday life, attire, cultural practices, and traditional occupations of various indigenous tribes from India's North-Eastern region. The portraits and candid scenes offer a window into tribal heritage, capturing moments such as weaving, adornment with traditional jewelry and headgear, community gatherings, and architectural styles like treehouses. Each framed photograph, arranged in a symmetrical grid on a softly lit wall, contributes to a visual narrative celebrating the rich diversity and identity of North-East India's tribal communities.

gallery.filename: Jain Votive Plaque made in spotted red sandstone, Kushana artefacts, National Museum, New Delhi 03.jpg
gallery.title: File:Jain Votive Plaque made in spotted red sandstone, Kushana artefacts, National Museum, New Delhi 03.jpg
gallery.source: Jain Votive Plaque made in spotted red sandstone, Kushana artefacts, National Museum, New Delhi 03
gallery.description:
Jain Votive Plaque made in spotted red sandstone in Mathura school of Art
"Two ayagapatas, the Sihanamdika Ayagapata (fig. 21) and the Acala Ayagapata (fig. 22), hint at the beginnings of standardization and regularity in their carvings which suggest a further maturation of the sculptural style of the first century A.D. The ornamental carving of these two plaques is rendered in a more regular, almost mechanical mode, lacking the organic dynamism of the late first century B.C. or the delicacy of the early first century A.D. Tightness and elongation begin to modulate the form of the seated Jina in the center of the Sihanamdika Ayagapata (fig. 2I), indicating a new trend in figural style. However, they do retain the richness of textures and softness of carving that betray their pre-second century A.D. date, as they are not as refined and crisp in style as the early second century A.D. Kusana material datable to the reign of Kaniska (fig. 33)" Ayagapatas: Characteristics, Symbolism, and Chronology p.116
